n: The Lord addresses Ezekiel as “son of man,” a title used over 90 times in this book. Here it stresses Ezekiel’s humble mortality before God’s glory. God tells him to stand up so they can speak.

f.g: Hebrew ben-adam: “human being, mortal.” In Ezekiel it marks the prophet’s lowliness; later it becomes a title of Christ.

n: The Spirit enters Ezekiel and lifts him to his feet. He cannot even stand in God’s presence without divine strength.
God sends Ezekiel to Israel—a people who, like their ancestors, have rebelled against him right up to the present.
The people are stubborn and hard-hearted, but Ezekiel’s job is simply to deliver God’s message: “Thus saith the Lord GOD.”

f.g: “Lord GOD” renders Adonai YHWH, Ezekiel’s favorite title for God (over 200 times).

n: Success is not measured by whether they listen. Whether they accept or refuse, they will know a true prophet was among them.

f.w: shall know that there hath been a prophet among them

n: Three times God says “be not afraid.” The people will be as painful as thorns and as dangerous as scorpions, but Ezekiel is not to be intimidated by their words or angry looks.

f.g: A picture of hostile, stinging opposition.

n: Ezekiel must speak God’s words faithfully, whatever the response.

f.w: thou shalt speak my words unto them

n: A test of the prophet himself: unlike rebellious Israel, Ezekiel must obey—beginning with eating whatever God gives him.

f.g: Ezekiel must model the obedience Israel lacked.

n: A hand reaches out to him holding a scroll.
The scroll is written on both sides—unusual, since scrolls normally had writing only inside—showing the message is full and complete. Its contents: laments, mourning, and woe for Israel.
